claims.text: Enriching Ta and V while depleting Mo and W in Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W alloys alters the electron concentration.
The altered electron concentration tunes bonding characteristics.
The altered electron concentration tunes phase stability.
Optimized elemental partitioning produces a refined and uniformly distributed microstructure.
A refined, uniformly distributed microstructure enhances dislocation mobility.
A refined, uniformly distributed microstructure limits stress concentration at potential fracture-initiation sites.
The compositional shift promotes enhanced solid-solution strengthening.
The resulting microstructure better accommodates dislocation motion.
The modified alloy will have improved yield strength.
The modified alloy will have improved ductility.
The modified alloy will have an improved Young's modulus.
The modified alloy will have improved fracture resistance or fracture toughness.
Strength is expected to improve by approximately 10–20% relative to the unmodified alloy processed under comparable conditions.
Fracture resistance is expected to improve by approximately 10–20% relative to the unmodified alloy processed under comparable conditions.
The predicted strength and fracture-resistance gains will occur without compromising ductility.
The modified alloy is expected to exhibit a modest increase in Young's modulus.
Controlled inert-atmosphere arc melting followed by homogenizing anneals minimizes microsegregation.
Controlled arc melting and homogenizing anneals ensure a uniform grain structure.
Undesirable phase separation or precipitation can override the intended effects of the composition change.
The predicted benefits may not occur when grain-boundary phenomena dominate mechanical behavior.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mechanism claim improved ductility, whereas the predicted outcome and falsification rule require only that ductility not be compromised. Thus the stated success criterion does not test the claimed ductility improvement.
